q: Which structure is the enol tautomer of cyclohexanone?
h: Tautomers differ only in where one H and one π bond sit: the H moves from the α-carbon to the carbonyl oxygen.
w: Keto–enol tautomerism moves one α-H to the carbonyl O and moves the π bond from C=O to C=C between the former carbonyl carbon and the α-carbon. The enol of cyclohexanone is cyclohex-1-en-1-ol, with the OH on an alkene carbon.
x: Here the OH is on an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon next to the C=C (an allylic alcohol). It is an isomer, but not an enol, and it cannot form from cyclohexanone by a single proton shift.
This is the enolate, the conjugate base. It has one fewer H than cyclohexanone, so it is not a tautomer.
Cyclohexene oxide has the same formula (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O) but a different carbon–oxygen connectivity; it is a constitutional isomer, not a tautomer.

q: 2-Methylcyclohexanone can form two different enols. Which enol is present in the larger amount at equilibrium?
h: Enols are alkenes. Which alkene-stability rule decides between the two enols?
w: An enol is an alkene, so the more substituted C=C is more stable (Zaitsev-type stability). Enolization toward C2 puts the C=C between C1 and the methyl-bearing C2, giving a tetrasubstituted enol. Enolization toward C6 gives only a trisubstituted C=C, so that enol is the minor one.
x: This is a real enol of 2-methylcyclohexanone, but its C=C is only trisubstituted, so it is less stable than the tetrasubstituted enol.
The OH is on an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon, so this is an allylic alcohol, not an enol; it is not a tautomer of the ketone.
The C=C is exocyclic to a carbon that does not carry the OH, so this is an allylic alcohol, not an enol.

q: Acetone contains far less than 0.01% enol at equilibrium, yet pure 2,4-pentanedione is roughly 80% enol. Which statement best explains the large enol content of 2,4-pentanedione?
c: The enol C=C is conjugated with the second C=O, and the enol OH forms a six-membered intramolecular hydrogen bond to that C=O.
An O–H bond is stronger than a C–H bond, which makes every enol more stable than its keto form; acetone simply enolizes too slowly to reach equilibrium.
The central CH<sub>2</sub> has a pK<sub>a</sub> near 9, so the compound exists mainly as its enolate, which is counted as enol.
Water and other protic solvents hydrogen-bond strongly to the enol OH, which is why the enol content is highest in polar solvents.
h: Look at the enol drawn on the right. What can its OH and C=C do with the remaining carbonyl that the enol of acetone cannot?
w: For simple ketones the keto form wins because a C=O π bond is much stronger than a C=C π bond. The enol of a β-diketone gains two extra stabilizations: the C=C–C=O system is conjugated, and the OH is held in a six-membered ring by an intramolecular hydrogen bond to the other carbonyl O. Together these outweigh the usual preference for the keto form.
x: If enols were generally more stable, acetone would be mostly enol at equilibrium; acid or base catalysis establishes that equilibrium quickly, and it lies far on the keto side.
Acidity (pK<sub>a</sub>) describes the enolate, not the neutral enol; with no base present the compound is neutral, and the enol/keto ratio is a separate equilibrium.
The opposite is observed: polar protic solvents compete for the hydrogen bond and lower the enol content (about 15% in water), which supports the intramolecular H-bond explanation.

q: Which labeled hydrogen-bearing carbon in ethyl acetoacetate carries the most acidic hydrogens?
h: Which carbon's conjugate base can spread the negative charge onto two carbonyl oxygens?
w: Removing H from carbon a, between the ketone and the ester C=O, gives an anion delocalized onto both carbonyl oxygens (pKa about 11). The methyl next to the ketone (d) is stabilized by only one C=O (pKa about 20), and the ethyl carbons (b, c) are not α to any carbonyl.
x: Carbon b is bonded to the ester oxygen, not to a carbonyl carbon; its anion has no resonance stabilization.
The terminal CH<sub>3</sub> of the ethyl group is an ordinary alkane-type C–H (pK<sub>a</sub> about 50).
The ketone methyl is α to one carbonyl only (pKa about 20); it is roughly a billion times less acidic than a.

q: Rank the compounds from least to most acidic (most acidic α-hydrogen in each).
h: Count the carbonyl groups that can share the negative charge, then ask whether a ketone C=O or an ester C=O is better at stabilizing an adjacent anion.
w: Typical pKa values: ethyl acetate (I) about 25, acetone (II) about 19–20, diethyl malonate (IV) about 13, 2,4-pentanedione (III) about 9. So I < II < IV < III. The ester OR group donates electrons into its own C=O by resonance, which makes that C=O less able to accept the enolate's negative charge; this is why esters are less acidic than ketones, and why a malonic ester (two ester groups) is less acidic than a β-diketone (two ketone groups).
x: This puts the ester above the ketone. Ester enolates are less stable because the alkoxy O already donates into the C=O, so an ester (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 25) is less acidic than a ketone (≈ 20).

This makes the malonic ester more acidic than the β-diketone. Each ester C=O stabilizes the anion less than a ketone C=O does, so malonate (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 13) is less acidic than 2,4-pentanedione (≈ 9).
Two ester carbonyls still beat one ketone carbonyl: diethyl malonate (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 13) is much more acidic than acetone (≈ 20).

q: Which labeled position carries the most acidic hydrogens?
h: Two of the labeled carbons are α to a carbonyl. Which type of carbonyl stabilizes an enolate better?
w: Carbons a and b are both α to a carbonyl, but a is α to a ketone (pKa about 19) while b is α to an ester (pKa about 25). The ester OCH3 donates into its own C=O, making the ester enolate less stable. So a is most acidic. Neither carbon is between two carbonyls (the carbonyls are 1,4-related), so there is no β-dicarbonyl effect.
x: Carbon b is α to the ester carbonyl; ester α-H's (pKa ≈ 25) are about a million times less acidic than ketone α-H's.
The OCH<sub>3</sub> hydrogens are on a carbon attached to oxygen, not to a carbonyl carbon; their conjugate base has no resonance stabilization.
Aryl C–H bonds have pK<sub>a</sub> near 43; the anion is in an sp<sup>2</sup> orbital perpendicular to the π system, so the C=O cannot stabilize it.

q: What is the major product of this sequence?
h: LDA is a strong, bulky base used cold and in a slight excess of base. Which α-H does it remove fastest, and is that step reversible?
w: LDA at −78 °C deprotonates quickly and irreversibly at the less hindered α-carbon (C6, a CH2), forming the kinetic enolate. SN2 attack on allyl bromide at that carbon gives 2-allyl-6-methylcyclohexanone (cis/trans mixture).
x: Alkylation at the methyl-bearing carbon comes from the more substituted (thermodynamic) enolate, which forms under equilibrating conditions such as NaOEt/EtOH, not with LDA at −78 °C.
Lithium enolates react with alkyl halides at carbon, not oxygen; the C-alkylated ketone is the normal product with soft electrophiles such as allyl bromide.
One equivalent of LDA forms one enolate per ketone; dialkylation at both α-carbons would require a second deprotonation and a second equivalent of halide.

q: LDA in THF at −78 °C converts 2-methylcyclohexanone mainly into the less substituted enolate, while NaOEt in ethanol at 25 °C gives mainly the more substituted enolate. Which explanation is correct?
c: LDA removes the less hindered H rapidly and irreversibly (kinetic control); with NaOEt, ketone and enolates interconvert by reversible proton transfer, so the more stable, more substituted enolate accumulates (thermodynamic control).
LDA removes the more acidic H on the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon, while NaOEt removes the less acidic H next to the methyl group because ethoxide is a weaker base.
Both bases give the same enolate mixture at first, but at −78 °C the more substituted enolate isomerizes to the less substituted one, which is more stable at low temperature.
Ethoxide is bulkier than LDA, so it can only reach the H on the methyl-bearing carbon, which is the less hindered position.
h: Compare pK<sub>a</sub> values: diisopropylamine about 36, ethanol about 16, ketone α-H about 19. Which base deprotonates reversibly?
w: LDA (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 36) deprotonates the ketone completely and irreversibly; the bulky base removes the more accessible H on C6 faster, and at −78 °C nothing equilibrates, so the kinetic (less substituted) enolate is formed. Ethoxide (EtOH pKa ≈ 16) is too weak to deprotonate completely (ketone pKa ≈ 19), so ketone, enolates and ethanol keep exchanging protons and the more substituted, more stable enolate dominates at equilibrium.
x: The two kinds of α-H have similar acidity; the difference comes from the rate of removal (sterics) versus the stability of the product enolate, not from one H being much more acidic.
At −78 °C there is no isomerization, and the less substituted enolate is the less stable one; low temperature preserves the kinetic product.
LDA, with two isopropyl groups on N, is far bulkier than ethoxide, and the methyl-bearing carbon is the more hindered position, not the less hindered one.

q: An enolate is alkylated with each of these halides. Which halide gives the poorest yield of C-alkylated product?
h: Enolate alkylation is an S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction. Which substrate cannot undergo S<sub>N</sub>2?
w: Enolate alkylation follows SN2 rules: methyl, primary, allylic and benzylic halides work well. A tertiary halide (2-bromo-2-methylpropane) cannot be attacked from the back side, and the strongly basic enolate instead causes E2 elimination to 2-methylpropene.
x: Methyl halides are the best S<sub>N</sub>2 substrates; enolate methylation with CH<sub>3</sub>I is fast and clean.
Benzylic halides are primary and their S<sub>N</sub>2 transition state is stabilized by the ring; they alkylate enolates very well.
Allylic halides are primary and activated toward S<sub>N</sub>2 by the adjacent π bond; they are excellent alkylating agents.

q: What is the major product when 2-methylcyclohexanone is treated with one equivalent of Br<sub>2</sub> in acetic acid?
h: Under acid, the halogen reacts with the enol. Which enol of this ketone is present in greater amount?
w: In acid the electrophile Br2 is attacked by the enol, and the more substituted (more stable) enol predominates. Bromination therefore occurs at the more substituted α-carbon, giving 2-bromo-2-methylcyclohexanone. The first Br withdraws electron density, making the carbonyl O less basic, so a second enolization (and a second bromination) is slow; acid-catalyzed halogenation stops after one halogen.
x: Bromination at C6 goes through the less substituted enol, which is the minor enol under acid; this product dominates under kinetic (LDA-type) conditions, not acid catalysis.
Acid-catalyzed halogenation stops after monohalogenation because the α-Br slows further enol formation; polyhalogenation is typical of base, not acid.
The methyl carbon is β to the carbonyl, not α; it cannot become part of an enol and is not brominated.

q: 1-Cyclohexylethan-1-one is treated with excess Br<sub>2</sub> in aqueous NaOH, and the mixture is then acidified. Which organic product (other than CHBr<sub>3</sub>) is isolated?
h: This is the haloform reaction. What happens to a CX<sub>3</sub> group attached to a carbonyl when hydroxide is present?
w: Under base each α-Br makes the remaining H on that carbon more acidic, so the methyl group is brominated three times to give a CBr3 ketone. Hydroxide then adds to the C=O, and the tetrahedral intermediate expels −CBr3 (stabilized by three Br). Proton transfer gives CHBr3 and the carboxylate, which acidification converts to cyclohexanecarboxylic acid.
x: Base-promoted halogenation does not stop at one halogen: the bromomethyl ketone is more acidic than the starting ketone and reacts faster.
Single halogenation at the more substituted α-carbon is the acid-catalyzed outcome; under base with excess Br<sub>2</sub> the methyl group is perhalogenated.
The tribromomethyl ketone is an intermediate; in aqueous NaOH it undergoes acyl substitution, losing <sup>−</sup>CBr<sub>3</sub> as the leaving group.

q: Acid-catalyzed bromination of acetone can be stopped cleanly at bromoacetone, but base-promoted bromination cannot: it continues to CH<sub>3</sub>COCBr<sub>3</sub>. Which single effect of the first α-Br explains both observations?
c: Its electron withdrawal makes the carbonyl O less basic (slowing acid-catalyzed enol formation) but makes the remaining α-H on that carbon more acidic (speeding enolate formation).
Its electron donation by resonance makes the carbonyl O more basic (speeding enol formation) but makes the α-H less acidic (slowing enolate formation).
Its large size blocks the approach of Br<sub>2</sub> in acid, while hydroxide is small enough to reach the remaining α-H.
It converts the ketone into an acid bromide, which cannot enolize in acid but enolizes rapidly in base.
h: The rate-determining step differs: forming the enol (after C=O protonation) in acid, removing α-H to form the enolate in base. How does an electronegative substituent affect each?
w: The rate-determining step in acid needs the carbonyl O to be protonated first. An α-Br is inductively electron-withdrawing, which lowers the basicity of the C=O oxygen, so enol formation from bromoacetone is slower than from acetone, and the reaction stops at one Br. In base the rate-determining step is removal of an α-H; the same electron withdrawal stabilizes the resulting enolate, so the CH2Br hydrogens are more acidic than those of acetone and each bromination accelerates the next, giving CBr3.
x: Resonance donation by Br into the C=O is minor here; the dominant effect is inductive withdrawal, and the observed trends (faster in base, slower in acid) are the opposite of what this choice predicts.
Steric bulk would slow halogenation in both media; it cannot explain why base halogenation speeds up after each Br.
The C–Br bond is on the α-carbon, not on the carbonyl carbon; bromoacetone is an α-halo ketone, not an acid bromide.

q: Each optically active compound is stirred in NaOH/H<sub>2</sub>O at 25 °C. Which one loses its optical activity?
h: Racemization through an enolate requires a stereocenter that both is an α-carbon and carries an H.
w: Base removes an α-H to form a planar enolate; reprotonation occurs equally from either face. Only a stereocenter that is α to the carbonyl and bears an H is destroyed this way. Only the ketone whose stereocenter is the α-carbon bearing an H racemizes.
x: The stereocenter is the β-carbon. Enolization involves only the α-CH<sub>2</sub>, so the configuration at the β-carbon is unchanged.
This stereocenter is α to the carbonyl but has no H (it carries CH<sub>3</sub>, ethyl and phenyl), so no enolate can form there.
This alcohol has no carbonyl group, so it cannot form an enol or enolate; the C–H at the stereocenter is not acidic.

q: 2-Methylcyclohexanone is stirred in D<sub>2</sub>O containing a catalytic amount of NaOD until no further change occurs. How many hydrogens are replaced by deuterium?
h: Only hydrogens on carbons directly attached to the C=O carbon exchange. Count them on both sides.
w: Exchange occurs through the enolate, so only α-H's are replaced. C2 has one H and C6 has two H's: 3 hydrogens become D. The methyl H's are on a β-carbon and do not exchange; neither do the ring H's at C3–C5.
x: This counts the methyl group or another non-α position. The methyl carbon is attached to C2, not to the carbonyl carbon, so its H's are β-H's.
Five would include all H's on C2, C3 and C6; C3 is a β-carbon and its H's are not acidic.
Two counts only C6. C2 also has one α-H; it is more hindered but still exchanges through the more substituted enolate under equilibrating conditions.
